title: Jeremiah 37:1–10
context: The narrator opens with Zedekiah, the king Nebuchadnezzar set on Judah’s throne in place of Coniah (compare 2 Kings 24:17, where his earlier name is given as Mattaniah), and states plainly that neither king, servants, nor people listened to the LORD’s words through Jeremiah. Zedekiah nevertheless sends messengers asking the prophet to pray (37:3); a similar delegation appears in 21:1–2 with partly different names, and the two scenes are named here without merging them. When Pharaoh’s army comes out of Egypt, the Babylonian (Chaldean) besiegers withdraw for a time (37:5). The LORD’s answer through Jeremiah (37:7–10) is that Egypt will go home and the Chaldeans will return to burn the city; 34:21–22 carries a related word. Both traditions read the Egyptian interlude as a test of whether Judah would trust a lull in the siege or the word of the LORD.

verses.text: Zedekiah the son of Josiah reigned as king instead of Coniah the son of Jehoiakim, whom Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon made king in the land of Judah.
verses.arminianNotes: The narrator says Zedekiah son of Josiah reigned in place of Coniah, made king by Nebuchadnezzar. Arminian readers note that Zedekiah’s throne itself depended on Babylon, setting up the pressures that shape his choices.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s hand behind the rise and fall of kings, even through a foreign ruler. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as historical setting, with 2 Kings 24:17 named as a parallel account of the same appointment.

verses.text: But neither he, nor his servants, nor the people of the land, listened to the LORD’s words, which he spoke by the prophet Jeremiah.
verses.arminianNotes: The narrator states that neither Zedekiah, his servants, nor the people listened to the LORD’s words through Jeremiah. Arminian readers see a shared refusal, king and people alike choosing not to heed what they heard.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the verse as a summary verdict on the reign, explaining the disaster that follows. Both traditions read the line as the key to the chapter: the word was spoken clearly, and the failure lay in not listening.

verses.text: Zedekiah the king sent Jehucal the son of Shelemiah and Zephaniah the son of Maaseiah, the priest, to the prophet Jeremiah, saying, “Pray now to the LORD our God for us.”
verses.arminianNotes: Zedekiah sends Jehucal and the priest Zephaniah to ask Jeremiah to pray for them. Arminian readers note the irony of seeking prayer while refusing the message, and see a king torn between fear and faith.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see a request for help that stops short of repentance. Shared ground: both traditions read the scene as real but half-hearted seeking, and they name the similar delegation in 21:1–2 without merging the two.

verses.text: Now Jeremiah came in and went out among the people, for they had not put him into prison.
verses.arminianNotes: The narrator notes that Jeremiah still moved freely among the people, not yet imprisoned. Arminian readers see this as setting the stage for the arrest to come, showing his freedom before it is taken away.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the narrator’s care with detail, which helps readers follow the prophet’s changing circumstances. Both traditions read the verse as background, marking the calm before Jeremiah’s suffering intensifies.

verses.text: Pharaoh’s army had come out of Egypt; and when the Chaldeans who were besieging Jerusalem heard news of them, they withdrew from Jerusalem.
verses.arminianNotes: Pharaoh’s army comes out of Egypt, and the Chaldeans lift the siege when they hear of it. Arminian readers see a moment of apparent relief that tempts Judah to think the danger has passed for good.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the withdrawal as a test permitted by God, revealing whether Judah would trust the prophetic word. Shared ground: both traditions read the Egyptian interlude as a pause that does not change the outcome the LORD had announced.

verses.text: Then the LORD’s word came to the prophet Jeremiah, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD’s word comes to the prophet Jeremiah. Arminian readers note that the prophet does not answer from his own judgment of the military situation but waits for a word from God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the formula as grounding what follows in divine authority, not political analysis. Both traditions read the verse as a reminder that Jeremiah’s message during the lull came from the LORD, not from his own reading of events.

verses.text: “The LORD, the God of Israel, says, ‘You shall tell the king of Judah, who sent you to me to inquire of me: “Behold, Pharaoh’s army, which has come out to help you, will return to Egypt into their own land.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD tells Jeremiah to say that Pharaoh’s army, which came to help, will return to Egypt. Arminian readers see a warning against trusting foreign alliances instead of the LORD, a theme found across the prophets.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God declaring the end of the Egyptian venture before it happens. Shared ground: both traditions read the word as exposing false hope in Egypt, and they note the king had sent to inquire of the LORD.

verses.text: The Chaldeans will come again, and fight against this city. They will take it and burn it with fire.” ’
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says the Chaldeans will return, fight against the city, take it, and burn it. Arminian readers note how clearly the outcome is stated, leaving the king no room to misunderstand.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the certainty of God’s announced judgment, later recorded in 39:8 and 52:13. Both traditions read the verse as a plain prediction of Jerusalem’s burning, and they name the later accounts without harmonizing their wording.

verses.text: “The LORD says, ‘Don’t deceive yourselves, saying, “The Chaldeans will surely depart from us;” for they will not depart.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD tells them not to deceive themselves by thinking the Chaldeans will surely leave. Arminian readers see a warning against wishful thinking, a self-deception people choose when the truth is hard.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the verse as exposing the heart’s tendency to believe what it wants. Shared ground: both traditions read the command as a call to face reality as God declares it, rather than comforting oneself with false hope.

verses.text: For though you had struck the whole army of the Chaldeans who fight against you, and only wounded men remained among them, they would each rise up in his tent and burn this city with fire.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says that even if only wounded Chaldeans remained, they would rise and burn the city. Arminian readers see vivid hyperbole stressing that Judah’s fate does not hang on military odds but on its relation to God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the hypothetical as underscoring the certainty of God’s decree, which no human strength can overturn. Both traditions read the image as removing every human ground for confidence, so that only the LORD’s word remains.
